Nov 25 : Pakistan International Airlines will move its UK operations to its own Boeing 777 fleet from November 26 after wet-lease partner Norse Atlantic Airways abruptly suspended operations, forcing the cancellation of two flights, the Pakistani carrier said on Wednesday. PIA said flights PK 786 from London Heathrow to Islamabad and PK 710 from Manchester to Lahore were cancelled after Norse Atlantic notified the airline of the suspension without prior warning as passengers were preparing to board.

Nov 25 : Dimorphos, the small asteroid struck by NASA's DART spacecraft in 2022 in the first test of a planetary defense system, was left with one side flattened with a stadium-sized crater and is tumbling in space, as shown by images taken by the European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft released on Wednesday. DART was sent on a proof-of-principle mission for using a spacecraft to change a celestial object's trajectory. Dimorphos, an oblong-shaped rocky object about 495 feet (151 meters) wide, orbits its companion asteroid Didymos, with a diameter of 2,395 feet (730 meters), and the pair is currently about 120 million miles (193.5 million km) from Earth. They are defined as near-Earth asteroids, though neither object imperils Earth. Previous data showed how DART succeeded in changing the path of Dimorphos — demonstrating that a spacecraft could alter the trajectory of an object headed toward a collision with Earth. Hera is now getting a close-up look at how DART physically changed Dimorphos. "The side impacted is now completely covered by a crater, with the visual impression that a piece of the asteroid was cut off by the impact. We do not see evidence for major changes on the site opposite to the DART impact. The combination of those two observations is surprising," Michael Kueppers, ESA's Hera mission scientist, told Reuters.

The big crater covers nearly the whole front side of Dimorphos as it continues its orbit of Didymos.  "Dimorphos is now tumbling in a chaotic way. There are hundreds of boulders floating around in the system," Kueppers said. Hera, about the size of a small car, is presently observing Didymos and Dimorphos from a distance of about 15 to 19 miles (25 to 30 km). Hera next month is slated to approach within 8 miles (13 km) of the pair, obtaining increasingly higher-resolution images.  In January, Hera is due to deploy two shoebox-sized miniature satellites, called CubeSats, that will approach even closer for further study, including investigating the interior structure of the two asteroids. Hera's mission manager unveiled the new images at a dinosaur hall in the Museum für Naturkunde Berlin as a reminder of the danger of asteroid impacts like the one 66 million years ago that caused a mass extinction on Earth and doomed the dinosaurs. The DART, short for Double Asteroid Redirection Test, spacecraft collided with Dimorphos on September 26, 2022, at about 14,000 miles per hour (22,530 kph). "We knew that the DART mission impacted Dimorphos successfully and that it changed its orbit. But we did not know what happened to Dimorphos itself. The investigation of what the impact did to Dimorphos and the characterization of it in general is needed to be able to apply the kinetic impactor technique to another asteroid, should we find one on a collision course with Earth," Kueppers said.

Source: Reuters

WASHINGTON, Nov 25 : The Federal Communications Commission is authorizing Elon Musk's SpaceX to deploy a constellation of 1 million satellites for data centers in space, the agency said on Wednesday. SpaceX earlier this year sought permission to deploy up to 1 million orbital compute modules to process massive amounts of data to be used on Earth. The FCC said it was approving the SpaceX “Starmind” constellation to help meet rapidly growing demand for AI computing. Under the license, SpaceX must begin deployment no later than November 2033, deploy 10 per cent of the maximum number — or 100,000 — no later than November 2035 and deploy 50 per cent by November 2038, the FCC said. Approving the application will permit SpaceX "to pioneer emergent technology that advances American leadership in space and artificial intelligence," the FCC added.

Data centers are the physical backbone of artificial intelligence, requiring massive amounts of power. "By directly harnessing near-constant solar power with little operating or maintenance costs, these satellites will achieve transformative cost and energy efficiency while significantly reducing the environmental impact associated with terrestrial data centers," SpaceX told the FCC. It was unclear whether SpaceX would put 1 million satellites in space, where only 17,000 satellites exist currently. Satellite operators sometimes request approval for higher numbers of satellites than they intend to deploy to buy design flexibility. SpaceX sought approval for 42,000 Starlink satellites before it began deployment of that system. The growing network currently has just over 11,000 satellites in space. SpaceX's request bets heavily on reduced costs of Starship, the company's next-generation reusable rocket under development, to help deploy satellites. Amazon's rival satellite unit Leo and others have criticized the plan, suggesting SpaceX was unlikely to deploy all the satellites and that it could take centuries to do so. FCC Chair Brendan Carr rejected that criticism in March. "Amazon should focus on getting Amazon's house in order with their own launches and their own satellite constellation, rather than worrying about other people that are actually out there launching satellites at the pace and cadence that SpaceX is," Carr said. The FCC said it was also approving SpaceX's requests to back up its optical network by approving additional communications.

Source: Reuters

NEW YORK: The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq retreated on Wednesday (Nov 25) amid a tech selloff, but finished well off the day's lows as bargain hunters stepped in ahead of the US Thanksgiving holiday. The Dow finished higher. The Nasdaq had been more than 4 per cent lower earlier in the session as the selloff in AI-related stocks and new US tariff proposals hit sentiment. "There are all these potential headwinds, but then there's also a certain amount of conditioning of buying on the dip, and that's part of what we're seeing," said Oliver Pursche, senior vice president and adviser for Wealthspire Advisors in Westport, Connecticut.

"The broad selloffs tend to kind of throw the baby out with the bathwater. Investors are taking advantage of some of those discrepancies," he said. Technology led declines among S&P 500 sectors, while materials and real estate were among top sector gainers. Wall Street has been roiled this month, partly because of worries about AI leader Nvidia. Jensen Huang resigned as CEO earlier this month, but the company's board reinstated him on Monday. The S&P 500 is down roughly 5 per cent for the month. Volume was lower than average ahead of the holiday. The market will be closed on Thursday and will close early on Friday. According to preliminary data, the S&P 500 lost 18.01 points, or 0.25 per cent, to end at 7,183.08 points, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 154.10 points, or 0.65 per cent, to 23,579.44. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 155.20 points, or 0.31 per cent, to 50,173.90. AI WORRIES WEIGH ON MARKET Nvidia shares fell along with an index of semiconductors as the tech selloff deepened. Fears of increased regulatory scrutiny of the AI sector following the Democratic sweep in the US midterm elections have added to worries about AI stocks . Early in the day, the Nasdaq 100 briefly fell 20 per cent from its record closing high, flirting with bear-market territory. Investors were also digesting news that the US proposed new tariffs on goods from 14 trading partners to combat what it calls structural excess industrial capacity, reviving global trade tensions. Data showed the US economy grew much faster than initially estimated in the third quarter, while inflation increased further in October, reinforcing expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates next month and again in early 2027. The extra tariffs could cloud the outlook for investors grappling with the prospect of interest rates staying higher for longer, as inflation has accelerated and oil prices have risen steadily due to the US-Iran war.

FAST

Nov 25 : Anthropic's slide below its initial public offering price has sharpened investor scrutiny of lofty technology valuations, as markets increasingly question whether even the biggest beneficiaries of the AI boom can generate enough profit to justify their price tags. Shares of the Claude developer were trading around $80.50, well below their $83 offer price and nearly 30 per cent below their opening price on November 19. The swift reversal highlights growing unease over how much investors are willing to pay for future growth, even as earnings prospects improve for many companies benefiting from artificial intelligence. Of the 86 Nasdaq-100 companies with positive earnings multiples and available earnings revision data, 60 saw their forward 12-month earnings forecasts rise over the past three months, a Reuters analysis of LSEG data showed. Yet, shares in 37 of those companies declined over the same period.

Nvidia shares have fallen about 25 per cent over the past three months despite a nearly 20 per cent increase in its earnings forecasts, partly driven by the volatile swings around CEO Jensen Huang's abrupt exit and reinstatement, while Marvell Technology and Lumentum have each lost more than 40 per cent of their market value even as earnings estimates rose 15 per cent and 20 per cent, respectively. HIGH EXPECTATIONS Despite the selloff, substantial valuation premiums persist. The 25 most richly valued companies in the Nasdaq-100 — many with exposure to AI, autonomous driving and other emerging technologies — traded at a median of 38 times projected earnings for the next 12 months, compared with 18 times for the remaining companies with positive earnings multiples, Reuters calculations showed. Anthropic illustrates how much future growth is already embedded in technology share prices. Morningstar's fair value estimate of $92 per share, just 12 per cent above Anthropic's latest closing price, assumes its annual revenue will increase nearly sevenfold over the next five years. Morningstar's estimates range from $25 to $188 per share under different scenarios, underscoring how sensitive Anthropic's valuation is to assumptions about future growth and profitability. The reassessment of valuations has been uneven across the tech sector. Forward price-to-earnings multiples for cybersecurity firms Fortinet and Palo Alto Networks rose the most over the past three months, climbing 11.5 per cent and 10.8 per cent, respectively. Multiples for Sandisk, Nvidia, Intuit Inc and Analog Devices contracted the most, falling between 15 per cent and 26 per cent, LSEG data showed. "Investors pay up for earnings they believe will last and discount those they think will fade," said Christopher Gannatti, global head of research at asset manager WisdomTree. Gannatti contrasted Palantir's high valuation with memory-chip maker Micron's much lower multiple, arguing that high memory prices could spur additional supply and eventually depress prices and profits. Palantir trades at 65 times forward earnings, compared with just 3.5 times for Micron, LSEG data showed. THE COST OF GROWTH The cost of delivering the growth implied by these valuations is another threat to future profitability. CoreWeave reported a 168 per cent rise in third-quarter revenue to $3.66 billion and a contracted revenue backlog of $132.5 billion. Yet the AI computing provider recorded a net loss of $709 million and expects capital spending of $37 billion to $39 billion this year. "Technological breakthroughs don't automatically translate into attractive returns on capital," said Troy Hooper, co-head of equity capital markets for the Americas at Mergermarket. "A year ago, investors were paying a much bigger premium for the promise of AI. Today, they're getting more tangible evidence of that promise and are seeking stronger profits." Growing competition could push down AI prices for customers, to the detriment of the companies investing heavily in the technology, Hooper said. Willis Tsai, head of global equities at Nuveen, said rising depreciation charges on AI chips and servers could erode cloud companies' profit margins even as demand for computing capacity grows.

(Reporting By Patturaja Murugaboopathy, Editing by Vidya Ranganathan and Nia Williams)

Source: Reuters

(Corrects attribution in paragraph 6) Nov 25 : The US Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network proactively took certain systems offline after a cybersecurity incident resulted in unauthorized access to a limited subset of the agency's systems, a FinCEN official said on Wednesday. The US Treasury Department is working with the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and third-party forensic examiners to determine the scope and impact, according to the official. Outages and disruptions across tech, government and other systems have become a growing concern for governments, companies and the public in recent months, as advanced AI tools make it easier to find vulnerabilities and attack systems.

Several technology failures this month have hit critical US systems, among them a nationwide halt to air travel, a Microsoft outage affecting email services, a glitch at several large banks and a brief disruption to the National Security Agency's network. "As a proactive measure, we have taken certain FinCEN systems offline and provided exceptive relief for filers that are not able to submit reports as a result of the disruption," the official said in a statement. While forensic analysis remains ongoing, there is no evidence of any breach of the Bank Secrecy Act or beneficial ownership databases, a person familiar with the matter said.

FAST

Nov 25 : AI-linked stocks were hammered for a second straight day on Wednesday, with investor concern about rising costs and forbidding debt dynamics sending the shares of many of the industry's largest players tumbling to fresh 52-week lows. AI lab Anthropic traded as low as $73.85 shortly after the open, putting it 11 per cent below its initial offering price last week. Alphabet dropped 4.7 per cent and hit a 52-week low that was some 35 per cent below its level at midyear. Chip giant Broadcom, one of the leaders of an epic midyear semiconductor rally, dropped 5.8 per cent and hit a 52-week low that left it 41 per cent below its high for 2026. The rout partly reflected the unwind of earlier optimism in the AI sector, driven in part by Democratic wins in US midterm elections that promise greater regulation and a slower, costlier AI buildout. Sentiment was further impaired on Wednesday by the Trump administration's proposed new tariffs on imports from 14 trading partners and data showing US inflation increased further in October. But the selling, which began soon after the Nasdaq composite's record high on October 6 and increased markedly in the second half of November, also underscored gathering concern about the financial underpinnings of an infrastructure expansion that has increasingly been financed by large sales of debt — a practice that tends to make markets more fragile and vulnerable to reversal.

Overnight in Tokyo, OpenAI shareholder SoftBank fell 14 per cent, underscoring fears that ChatGPT maker OpenAI may face increasing resistance as it seeks to raise money. SoftBank, also a major investor in chip firm Arm, is down more than 40 per cent for the year. Nvidia, a major OpenAI partner in data centers and other aspects of the AI ecosystem, dropped 8.5 per cent to a fresh low. The so-called neocloud firms that back AI data center capacity were under renewed attack, reflecting in part concern about their capacity to raise funds to support ambitious building plans. "It seems that these companies are trying to one-up each other on the amount of money that they're spending, but you have to show that it's worth it, and that's where Wall Street is saying 'I don't know'," said Todd Schoenberger, chief investment officer at CrossCheck Management. HEADING INTO BEAR TERRITORY The Nasdaq-100 was down 4 per cent by mid-morning. The index briefly fell 20 per cent below its October 6 record closing high, a level that would confirm a bear market if it held through Wednesday's close. The worries about the underpinnings of the AI boom were so significant that even firms reporting strong results were caught in the downdraft, reflecting in part their large stock-price gains earlier in the year. Dell Technologies fell 5.7 per cent on Wednesday despite the server maker raising its annual revenue and profit forecasts for the third time this year and approving an additional $25 billion share buyback. Dell stock has more than doubled for the year. Rival AI server maker HPE tumbled 16.3 per cent on Tuesday after raising its full-year revenue outlook. Shares of Ambarella, valued at $2 billion, tumbled 20.9 per cent after the AI semiconductor firm forecast fourth-quarter revenue below analysts' estimates. The Philadelphia chips index slid 7 per cent to hit a more than seven-month low. The index has plunged more than 43 per cent from its record high in June. Shares of AI hyperscalers were broadly lower, with Oracle down 8 per cent and Amazon.com off 6 per cent. Nvidia-backed neocloud firms CoreWeave and Nebius Group fell more than 10 per cent each, while IREN, Applied Digital and Core Scientific lost between 6.9 per cent and 10.8 per cent. Neocloud providers, which rent out specialized AI computing capacity, have been under pressure since October over concerns about the debt funding their rapid expansion. The yield on CoreWeave's bonds due 2031 rose to almost 18 per cent as prices fell nearly 2 cents on the dollar to near record lows, Tradeweb data showed. The cost of insurance against tech companies defaulting on debts has jumped sharply, with five-year CDS spreads at Oracle, Alphabet, SpaceX and CoreWeave hitting record levels.

MUMBAI, Nov 25 : Indian fintech PhonePe has resumed preparations for its initial public offering and is targeting a listing in the first three months of next year at a valuation of $12 billion to $15 billion, a person directly aware of the discussions said. The Walmart-backed company is expected to file its updated draft papers with India's market regulator, the Securities and Exchange Board of India, within the next 30 to 45 days, the person said, requesting anonymity as talks are confidential. The listing is set to be India's biggest fintech debut since Paytm's $2.5 billion float in 2021. PhonePe had paused its listing plans in March due to global capital market volatility stoked by geopolitical tensions in the Middle East. The issue will be an entirely secondary share sale to raise $1.2 billion to $1.5 billion, retaining the size outlined in PhonePe's January draft prospectus, where majority owner Walmart said it would trim its stake by about 12 per cent, and investors Tiger Global and Microsoft planned to fully exit.

BRUSSELS, Nov 25 : A European Union meeting expected to consider Tesla's bid for bloc-wide approval of its assisted self-driving system has been postponed until December 15, a European Commission spokesperson told Reuters on Wednesday. The Technical Committee for Motor Vehicles (TCMV) had been expected to consider, and potentially vote on, the system at its December meeting after no vote was held at two earlier meetings following preliminary approval from the Netherlands in April. Tesla Assisted Driving (TAD), renamed from Full Self-Driving (FSD) as a result of concerns from regulators, is a so-called "hands-off, eyes-on" system that can steer, accelerate and brake while requiring constant supervision from the driver. The vote is a key hurdle in Tesla's effort to roll out the technology across Europe. Nearly a dozen countries have followed the Dutch lead, with Italy the most populous to begin a rollout. But EU-wide approval requires backing from at least 15 of the bloc's 27 member states representing 65 per cent of its population. A rejection at EU level would invalidate the national approvals already granted. The meeting had originally been scheduled for December 1, Dutch regulator RDW told Reuters. Belgium's Flanders transport ministry initially said it had been moved to December 7 before the Commission clarified that it would instead take place on December 15.

LONDON, Nov 25 : Online fast-fashion retailer Shein warned on Wednesday that its European business could take a year to recover as e-commerce import fees hit sales in its biggest market and dragged down group revenue. Shein's third-quarter results are the first to show the impact of the European Union's €3 ($3.28) fee on e-commerce imports, which has eroded its competitive edge just as the newly listed company seeks to bolster confidence in its business model. CEO Sky Xu said sales in Europe might not recover until the second half of 2027, when most deliveries would be made from European warehouses the company is investing in. "We expect the EU to remain under pressure for the next few quarters," Xu said on a call with analysts.

Revenue in Europe fell 27.6 per cent to $2.98 billion in the quarter after Shein raised prices to offset the additional costs. Shein also faces an uncertain year-end shopping season after the EU began imposing an additional €2 fee on e-commerce parcels at the start of November. The charges apply to each type of item in a shipment, meaning a Shein order containing five different items could incur customs fees of €25, a hefty hit for a retailer that grew popular by selling €5 dresses and €10 shoes. Once one of the fastest-growing online retailers, Shein helped intensify price competition for established rivals such as H&M and Zara. But its rapid expansion has stalled since the US and Europe removed duty-free access for e-commerce imports. Group revenue fell 6 per cent to $10.27 billion, reflecting weaker sales in Europe and a 9.4 per cent decline in the US. SHEIN EYES LATIN AMERICA FOR GROWTH Facing a sharp slowdown in sales, Shein cut marketing spending by 41.5 per cent in the quarter, reducing online advertising to protect profitability. Operating income rose 17 per cent from a year earlier to $743 million. Xu sought to reassure investors that Shein was growing rapidly in other regions, particularly Latin America, reducing its dependence on Europe and the US. The share of sales generated outside Europe and the US rose to nearly 50 per cent in the quarter, with revenue from the rest of the world up 18 per cent to $4.2 billion. "Consumers around the world are becoming more cautious," Xu said, adding that providing value for money remained critical. ($1 = 0.9136 euros)

LONDON, Nov 25 : Retailers heading into the Black Friday shopping period face growing cyber threats as artificial intelligence makes attacks faster and more potent, at a time when the sector has some of the lowest levels of cyber insurance protection. The post-Thanksgiving spree has long represented a lucrative sales opportunity, but more frequent and sophisticated cyberattacks are increasingly testing retailers' cyber resilience. Ransomware attacks on retail, leisure and hospitality businesses are 50 per cent more frequent in November than the monthly average, according to claims data from insurer CFC. Only 43 per cent of small and medium-sized retailers carry cyber insurance, compared with 81 per cent in financial services and 71 per cent in technology. "Retailers spend months making sure their websites, stock and logistics can withstand the surge in customers. But Black Friday should be treated as a resilience exercise as much as a revenue opportunity," said Lindsey Maher, CFC's head of global cyber development.

Black Friday and Cyber Monday bookend one of the retail sector's busiest periods of the year, with consumers searching for deals and retailers often offering hefty discounts. UK shoppers looking to snap up bargains are set to spend £235 ($307) each this Black Friday, with UK spending expected to reach its highest since 2022, research from PwC shows. Retailers don't generally buy additional cyber insurance for a weekend and focus instead on testing and strengthening resilience, said David Molony, Europe, Middle East and Africa head of cyber and financial sponsors at Aon. That matters most at a time of year when revenue depends heavily on technology, he said. "A cyber incident that interrupts the ability to trade during peak season can move very quickly from an operational issue to a material financial loss," he said. US retailer Target incurred net cumulative expenses of $202 million after a 2013 breach during the holiday shopping season that compromised at least 40 million credit cards, the company has said. Complex retail supply chains, copious credit card records and the busy shopping period mean retailers are primed for maximum chaos and interruption, said Sydonie Williams, head of international cyber risks at Beazley. While AI increases the threat risk, it also improves defence mechanisms, she said. Francisco Donoso, chief product and technology officer at Beazley Security, said AI was speeding up attacks and the number of vulnerabilities being exposed was almost six times higher than a year ago. "It's really hard for organisations to keep up," Donoso said. ($1 = 0.7639 pounds)

Investors are nervous about the geopolitical tension going into the weekend, said Phil Flynn, an analyst at Price Futures Group.  US CRUDE STOCKS RISE LESS THAN ANTICIPATED US crude stocks rose by 1.1 million barrels to 418.9 million barrels in the week ended November 20, the Energy Information Administration said. Analysts in a Reuters poll expected a 1.5 million-barrel rise. [EIA/S]  The inventory report pushed prices higher as the market was expecting a bigger inventory build, Flynn said.  The uncertainty surrounding OPEC+ ahead of its November 29 meeting, where they will decide on their 2027 output policy, has held prices in check. The United Arab Emirates is no longer restricted by OPEC+ policies, and Iraq is looking to boost its oil capacity, said Zhenqiang Seto, an oil research specialist at LSEG. OPEC+ ministers will hold a series of meetings on November 29. "Since the release of an IEA report this month, perceptions of a global supply glut have kept prices in check," said Tsuyoshi Ueno, senior economist at NLI Research Institute. Attention is also focused on how next year's production quotas will be determined at the OPEC+ meeting, Ueno added. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said OPEC+ is set to complete a review of member production capacities by year-end. Iraq and Kazakhstan were pressing OPEC+ to raise its estimate of their oil production capacity, said four people familiar with the matter, heightening tensions over a review that will help determine how much members can pump next year.    Libya's Sharara oil pipeline reopened, ending a brief halt after what the National Oil Corporation described as an unlawful group closed a valve.  In the Strait of Hormuz, a container ship was targeted and came to a stop on Tuesday while sailing an "unauthorised" route near the strait, Iran's Revolutionary Guards told state media.

Nov 25 : Flipkart CEO Kalyan Krishnamurthy will step down after nearly a decade at the helm of one of India's largest e-commerce companies, while the Walmart-owned retailer prepares for a potential stock market listing amid intense competition. Krishnamurthy steered Flipkart through its $16 billion acquisition by Walmart in 2018 and a period of rapid expansion that cemented its position in the market. Its rivals include Amazon and a new generation of quick-commerce and online retail players. "I believe an anchor is out. And that's a big anchor to miss," said Harish Bijoor, a business and brand-strategy specialist. Chief product and technology officer Balaji Thiagarajan will lead Flipkart in the interim, the company said on Wednesday, adding that it would announce a successor in the coming weeks.

Flipkart had announced in March that group finance chief Sriram Venkataraman would step down. "Considering Flipkart's leadership in the India market, it's going to be difficult for anyone to come and step in so easily to succeed Krishnamurthy," said Anil Kumar, founder and CEO of consumer and internet-focused consulting firm Redseer Strategy Consultants. Krishnamurthy's association with Flipkart predates his executive career at the company. In 2011, he joined investment firm Tiger Global — an early investor in Flipkart — and represented the firm on the e-commerce company's board before joining Flipkart in 2016. He became CEO in January 2017 and group CEO in 2018, the year Walmart acquired a roughly 77 per cent stake in the company in one of the largest deals in India's technology sector. Founded in 2007, Flipkart has more than 500 million registered users. It has played a significant role in shaping India's online retail market, expanding access to products beyond major cities and building capabilities in payments, logistics and digital commerce.
